messages.subject: Bayesian Model Based inference question
parts:
Hi, 

working my way through converting the example of Model-based inference analysis from Buckland et al (2015) at https://examples.distancesampling.org/book-bobwhite/bobwhite.html#defining-the-likelihood-function by Cornelia Oedekoven for my line-transect data. 

How does one choose the initial values for the MH updating algorithm? 

I understand that I can use similar values as the example for the upper and lower distribution limits and then pilot tune it later, but I'm not sure the where the logic behind each of the initial values for the MH updating algorithm come from, and as such, I'm struggling to convert it for my dataset. For instance, how were the initial values for the covariate coefficients (type and state) chosen? 

From the example: 
######### 2.4. Initial Values for the MH updating algorithm #########

## initial values for the detection function parameters  
# MCDS with covariates type and state
# scale intercept and shape (enter the model on the log-scale)
sig.0<-log(130) # the scale intercept
sha.0<-log(2.5) # shape parameter
# type coefficient
sigtr.0<-0.2    # level treat
# state coefficients 
sigms.0<- 0.61  # MS
signc.0<- 0.66  # NC
sigtn.0<- 0.47  # TN

## initial values for count model parameters
int.0<- -13     # intercept
# type coefficient
typ.0<- 0.4     # level treat
# Julian Date coefficient (covariate JDctr)
day.0<- -0.01   # continuous covariate
# state coefficients
stms.0<- 0.014  # state MS
stnc.0<- -0.38  # state NC
sttn.0<- -1.36  # state TN
# random effects standard deviation and coefficients
std.ran.0<-log(1)
j=183 # number of sites in covey data (j = length(covey.data$Tj))
set.seed(1234)
raneff<-rnorm(j,0,exp(std.ran.0))
# combining the initial values in a single array 
# for input into the covey.full.bayes.log.lik function 
curparam<-c(sig.0,sha.0,sigtr.0,sigms.0,signc.0,sigtn.0,
            int.0,typ.0,day.0,stms.0,stnc.0,sttn.0,std.ran.0)



Any help would be greatly appreciated!

messages.author: eb8cb2a1b9414adb
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Bayesian Model Based inference question
parts:
Hi Scarlett,  

 

Great to hear you are working through the example. Regarding your question about how to choose the starting values for the MH algorithm: first you need to think about if there is a range of values that these need to fall into for the respective parameter. For example, the scale parameter of the detection function (half-normal or hazard-rate) needs to be larger than zero. After that, in theory, any values should work. However, the further this value is from what the chain will eventually converge on, the longer the chain will take to converge. To narrow down the range of options you can also think about what might make sense biologically (when dealing with biological data) and essentially have a guess at what this parameter value might be. For example, the scale parameter of a half-normal detection function will define how quickly the estimated detection probabilities drop off as distance increases. For small values, the estimated detection probabilities drop off very quickly, i.e. you have low detection probabilities at small distances, and vice versa. Here you could simply plot a detection function using a candidate starting value and see if it would make sense biologically. For example, if you plot a half-normal detection function with a scale parameter of 100 (using meters), it yields a detection probability of ~0.9 at distance 50m. Can I really expect to detect 90% of my study species at 50m? If that is too high, you can try a smaller value, and so on. You can do this for each parameter. A “quick and dirty” method to find starting values is to find the maximum likelihood parameter estimates and use these. However, remember that you should always conduct a sensitivity analysis where you test different starting values. Hope this helps!  

 

Cornelia

messages.author: eb8cb2a1b9414adb
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Bayesian Model Based inference question
parts:
Hi Scarlett, 

 

I thought of one more thing: when you consider the starting values for the parameters associated with the covariates in the count model, you have to remember that they are modelled via the log-link function in our case. So, for example if you think about what a good starting value for the type covariate is, you will have to take this into account. The way you do this is, e.g., if you consider a starting value of 0.4 for the type covariate, you will have to consider that this value is associated with the level ‘treat’. To determine if this makes sense biologically, you have to see what effect this value would have on the response level. For this, you convert it back using exp(0.4) = 1.491825. This means that on treated fields we expect counts to be on average ~49% higher than on control fields. Here, the base-level type=control is absorbed in the intercept. Similarly, for the state covariate, one state (the base-level) is absorbed in the intercept and the others are compared with this baseline. For example, a starting value of 0.014 for state MS means that we expect counts to be ~1.4% higher in the state MS (exp(0.014) = 1.014098) than in the state of the base-level.  

 

Cornelia
